transcript.question: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?
transcript.answer: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. My work involves adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and sending drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back afterwards.

transcript.question: When you arrive at the start of a typical shift, what is the very first thing you do, and how does the rest of your day usually unfold?
transcript.answer: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, and I handle tasks like adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are ready, and send drones to charge. My notes do not state what the very first thing I do is when I arrive at the start of a shift, or how the rest of my day unfolds.

transcript.question: Who hands work to you during the day, and who do you hand drones or updates over to when you finish a task?
Can you tell me about the worst day you have had at work over the last few months, and what made it so bad?
Is there anything you check by hand today because you do not trust the information or systems you currently have?
When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?
What are you most worried a new software service might get wrong or make harder in your work?
transcript.answer: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. I also worry that the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction may get through twice and the sender often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

transcript.question: Can you give a concrete example of what goes wrong in your work when an instruction gets through twice or a report from a drone arrives late or out of order?
You mentioned taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back afterwards—how does that process work for you?
transcript.answer: I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians like me, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

transcript.question: When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you need to show them?

You mentioned adding new drones to the fleet and retiring old ones—what happens when you do either of those?

What is involved when you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge?
transcript.answer: I add new drones to the fleet and retire old ones, and each of our company's drones has a home site. I also set up charging pads at our sites, and we have a few dozen of them which are never lent to another company. Each drone uses a specific charging connector type that is not interchangeable, and I send drones to charge.

transcript.question: What do you need to check or know before you send a drone to charge at one of your sites?
What else can you tell me about the drones, the sites, or the charging pads that affects how you do your job?
transcript.answer: We run a few dozen charging pads at our sites, and they are never lent to another company. Our company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, which differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, their sensors, and their charging connectors. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.

transcript.question: What else do you run into with batteries, repairs, or keeping track of drones across your sites?
transcript.answer: Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Each drone has a home site.

transcript.answer: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and each of our drones has a home site. We run a few dozen charging pads at our sites, and they are never lent to another company. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable.

transcript.question: Walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish.
transcript.answer: I plan and run our flights, and as a licensed dispatcher, I am responsible for each flight by deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off before it leaves. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. Before and outside my control, things happen like loads being ready or not, and drones reaching their points and arriving.

transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace. This includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
